The Davisson-Germer Experiment. In 1927, two physicists named Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer fired a beam of electrons at a nickel crystal and observed something that seemed impossible. The electrons behaved like waves, not particles. This result proved a bold theoretical prediction and changed how we understand matter itself.

Davisson and Germer had initially set out to study how electrons scatter off crystal surfaces. An accident helped them. A heating episode altered the nickel's crystalline structure, and when they repeated their measurements, they saw an unexpected pattern.

Electrons scattered at certain angles with maxima and minima—the distinctive diffraction pattern of waves passing through a crystal lattice. It was the same kind of pattern you see when light passes through a slit, creating alternating bright and dark bands.

Using Bragg's law, which describes how X-rays diffract through crystal structures, they calculated the wavelength of the electron beam from the diffraction pattern. And the wavelength matched perfectly with a prediction made by Louis de Broglie four years earlier. De Broglie had hypothesized that all matter carries a wave character, with wavelength equal to Planck's constant divided by momentum.

The experiment required only electron energies of fifty to one hundred fifty volts, low enough to be practical. Yet the wavelengths were around a tenth of a billionth of a meter—comparable to atomic spacings and perfect for revealing the wave nature of matter.

George Thomson, the son of the physicist who had discovered the electron as a particle, independently confirmed electron diffraction at around the same time. His confirmation solidified the reality of the effect. Electrons are both particles and waves, and the Davisson-Germer experiment proved it experimentally.
